clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive form of congenital stationary night blindness, most commonly caused by RDH5 mutations that impair the visual (retinoid) cycle
Fundus shows numerous discrete white or yellow-white dots scattered across the retina, sparing the fovea and typically densest in the mid-periphery and posterior pole
Night blindness is present from early life; crucially the course is usually stationary, distinguishing it from progressive retinitis punctata albescens
The hallmark functional feature is markedly delayed dark adaptation: rod (and often cone) responses are subnormal initially but recover toward normal after a very prolonged period of dark adaptation
On standard electroretinography rod responses are reduced, but they improve substantially after extended dark adaptation, reflecting slow regeneration of visual pigment

Fundus autofluorescence and optical coherence tomography help characterise the dots and confirm relative structural preservation, in contrast to the degenerative changes of retinitis punctata albescens
Management is supportive with reassurance about the stationary course and genetic counselling, though some cases develop late macular or cone dysfunction requiring monitoring
reference.pathophysiology: Fundus albipunctatus is most often caused by recessive mutations in RDH5, which encodes 11-cis retinol dehydrogenase, an enzyme of the retinal pigment epithelium visual cycle. Deficiency slows regeneration of 11-cis retinal and therefore of rhodopsin, so photoreceptors recover very slowly after light exposure, producing night blindness and markedly delayed dark adaptation. Accumulation of retinoid intermediates in the retinal pigment epithelium is thought to underlie the characteristic white dots. Because the photoreceptors themselves are largely preserved, the disorder is usually stationary, unlike the progressive degeneration of retinitis punctata albescens.
additionalDifferentials: Retinitis punctata albescens (progressive, with pigmentary degeneration)
Other forms of congenital stationary night blindness
Drusen or flecked retina syndromes (for example fundus flavimaculatus)
additionalInvestigations: Prolonged dark adaptometry demonstrating delayed but eventual rod recovery
Full-field electroretinography before and after extended dark adaptation
Fundus autofluorescence and optical coherence tomography to characterise the white dots and assess structural integrity
Colour vision and visual field testing
Molecular genetic testing (RDH5 and related visual-cycle genes)
Serial assessment to detect any late cone or macular involvement
redFlags: Progressive field loss, pigmentary change or acuity decline suggesting retinitis punctata albescens rather than the stationary disorder
Late-onset macular dysfunction reducing central acuity
Systemic features or malabsorption suggesting acquired vitamin A deficiency
Affected siblings requiring screening given recessive inheritance
reference.prognosis: Generally good, as the disorder is typically stationary with preserved daytime acuity; a minority develop late cone dystrophy or macular changes that can reduce central vision.
pitfalls: Confusing it with progressive retinitis punctata albescens and giving an incorrectly poor prognosis
Recording a reduced rod electroretinogram without repeating it after prolonged dark adaptation and missing the diagnostic recovery
Overlooking late cone or macular involvement on follow-up
Mistaking the white dots for drusen or a flecked retina dystrophy
management: No specific pharmacotherapy exists; management centres on reassurance and counselling that the disorder is usually stationary with preserved daytime acuity
Advise on the practical impact of night blindness and markedly delayed dark adaptation, with caution over night driving and provision of low-vision aids and lighting adaptations
Long-term ophthalmological surveillance with serial optical coherence tomography, fundus autofluorescence and electroretinography to detect any late cone dystrophy or macular involvement
Periodic colour vision and visual field assessment to monitor for progression
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder, with cascade testing of at-risk relatives for RDH5 and related visual-cycle variants
Referral to clinical genetics and low-vision rehabilitation services as part of multidisciplinary care
